title: Coconut Oil vs Olive Oil: Why Their Nutrition Is So Different

seo.title: Coconut Oil vs Olive Oil: Key Differences
seo.meta_description: Coconut oil has about 82 g saturated fat per 100 g versus roughly 14 g in olive oil. Calories are similar, but the fatty-acid profiles are very different.
seo.search_intent: Compare coconut and olive oil by saturated fat, calories, and everyday use.

excerpt: Both oils provide about 120 calories per tablespoon, but their fat profiles are very different: coconut oil is about 82% saturated fat by weight, while olive oil is around 14%. Olive oil is therefore much richer in unsaturated fat for everyday use.
content_html:
Coconut oil and olive oil have almost the same calories because both are essentially pure fat, yet their fatty-acid profiles are very different. Coconut oil is predominantly saturated fat, while olive oil is predominantly monounsaturated fat. That distinction matters more nutritionally than smoke-point marketing or the idea that one oil is “natural” and the other is not. Coconut oil can have a useful flavor and texture in specific dishes, but olive oil is the stronger everyday default when the goal is to replace saturated fat with unsaturated fat.

The saturated-fat gap is large even though calories match

USDA composition data put coconut oil at roughly 82 grams of saturated fat per 100 grams, compared with about 14 grams in olive oil. On a tablespoon scale, coconut oil supplies around 11–12 grams of saturated fat while olive oil provides roughly 2 grams. Both still deliver close to 120 calories per tablespoon. Switching from coconut to olive oil therefore does not make the spoonful low-calorie; it mainly changes the type of fatty acids you are eating.

Olive oil's main fat is oleic acid

Olive oil is rich in oleic acid, a monounsaturated fatty acid. Extra-virgin olive oil also retains phenolic compounds and flavor components from the fruit because it is obtained mechanically rather than refined to neutrality. Research on Mediterranean-style dietary patterns gives olive oil, especially extra-virgin olive oil, a much stronger evidence base as a routine culinary fat than coconut oil. That evidence does not mean every tablespoon produces a special health effect by itself; it supports a broader pattern in which unsaturated fats replace some saturated fats.

Coconut oil's texture and flavor explain why cooks use it

Its high saturated-fat content makes coconut oil solid or semi-solid at temperatures where olive oil remains liquid. That can be useful in vegan baking, confectionery, curries, granola, or recipes where coconut flavor is desired. Refined coconut oil has a more neutral flavor than virgin coconut oil. Those are legitimate culinary reasons to choose it. The problem comes when a specialty fat is promoted as nutritionally superior simply because it is plant-derived or because some of its fatty acids are medium-chain. Commercial coconut oil is not the same as purified medium-chain triglyceride oil.

Both oils can be used for ordinary cooking

Extra-virgin olive oil is suitable for sautéing, roasting, pan cooking, dressings, and many frying applications at normal household temperatures. Smoke point is only one characteristic of an oil and does not by itself predict overall stability or healthfulness. Coconut oil is also heat-stable enough for many cooking uses, partly because of its saturated-fat content. The question is therefore not whether coconut oil “survives heat” better; it is whether its flavor, texture, and fatty-acid profile make sense for the dish and your overall diet.

Replacing saturated fat is the key nutritional comparison

Major health guidance recommends limiting saturated fat and replacing some of it with unsaturated fats rather than simply adding more fat. If coconut oil replaces butter, the saturated-fat reduction may be small because both are high in saturated fatty acids. If olive oil replaces coconut oil or butter, the shift toward monounsaturated fat is much larger. That replacement framing is more informative than asking which oil has more vitamins or which has a higher smoke point.

Use olive oil as the routine option and coconut for a reason

If you enjoy coconut flavor in a curry or need a semi-solid plant fat in a particular recipe, coconut oil can fit. If you need one versatile oil for vegetables, sauces, dressings, grains, fish, meat, and everyday stovetop cooking, olive oil offers a more favorable unsaturated-fat profile and a deeper evidence base. The two oils are equally energy-dense, but they are not nutritionally equivalent: olive oil is far lower in saturated fat, while coconut oil is best treated as a specific culinary fat rather than a default health oil.

faq.question: Which has more calories?
faq.answer: They are nearly the same, at roughly 120 calories per tablespoon.

faq.question: Why is coconut oil solid?
faq.answer: Its high saturated-fat content makes it solid or semi-solid at temperatures where olive oil remains liquid.

faq.question: Does coconut oil contain cholesterol?
faq.answer: Plant oils contain no cholesterol, but coconut oil is very high in saturated fat, which can raise LDL cholesterol.
